summary: Another revision of the Network Working Group's documentation conventions, updating RFC 10, RFC 16 and RFC 24. It restates how notes in the series are produced and shared. A later revision appears in RFC 30.

eli5.summary: This is another updated version of the rules for writing and sharing notes in the group.

questions: what was the network working group
subtitle: The early rules for writing Network Working Group notes: timely, informal and open to anyone.

tldr.problem: The Network Working Group needed a simple way to document its work on HOST software and network strategies, and people hesitated to publish unpolished ideas.
tldr.mechanism: Notes may come from anyone and cover any thought about the network, must carry a standard header (serial number, author, date, title), and are mailed to a list of 12 people.
tldr.outcome: It revises RFC 10, 16 and 24 and was itself updated by RFC 30.

sections.title: The Network Working Group and Its Notes
sections.content:
This note revises RFC 10, RFC 16 and RFC 24. The Network Working Group (NWG) consists of interested people from existing or potential ARPA network sites, and membership is not closed. It is concerned with HOST software, the strategies for using the network, and initial experience with the network.

The group's work is documented in notes like this one, which may be produced by anybody at any site and included in the series.
sections.eli5: A club of people connecting computers writes little notes to each other, and anyone may write one.

sections.title: What a Note May Contain
sections.content:
A note may hold any thought or suggestion related to HOST software or another aspect of the network. Notes should be timely rather than polished. Philosophical positions without examples, suggestions without background, and questions without attempted answers are all acceptable, and the minimum length is one sentence.

The standards are stated openly for two reasons: a written statement tends to be seen as authoritative, and the group wants to promote discussion of far less authoritative ideas, and to ease the natural hesitancy to publish something unpolished.
sections.eli5: Half-baked ideas are welcome. Even one sentence counts, so nobody should feel shy.

sections.title: Required Form
sections.content: Every note should carry four items: the words Network Working Group and Request for Comments: X where X is a serial number assigned by Steve Crocker at UCLA, the author and affiliation, the date, and a title. The title need not be unique.
sections.eli5: Each note needs a number, who wrote it, when, and a name.

sections.title: Distribution
sections.content: The author's site sends one copy to each of 12 named people at MIT, Utah, SDC, UCLA, SRI, MITRE, RAND, BB&N, Raytheon, ARPA, Lincoln Laboratory and UCSB. Further reproduction may be handled locally. The note also lists the addresses and phone numbers on file for each person and asks recipients to correct them.
sections.eli5: The writer mails one copy to twelve people, and they copy it for others if they want.

references.text: Documentation conventions, NWG/RFC 10, revised by this note.
